safetyNote: Do not eat Agaricus pilatianus. Species accounts describe it as poisonous and capable of severe gastrointestinal cramps. Its chrome-yellow staining at the stem base and phenolic or iodine-like odour are warning signs, but neither a single colour nor smell test safely excludes toxic Agaricus. Have suspected ingestions with symptoms assessed by a poison centre.

sections.title: Identification
sections.text: A stocky Agaricus with a fleshy cap about 6–12 cm across, convex then expanded. The cap may be dirty white when young but often becomes smoky grey-brown, fibrillose-squamulose to more distinctly scaly, with an irregular scaly margin. Crowded free gills are pale at first, then pink and finally chocolate brown; the spore deposit is dark brown. It must not be assumed to be a familiar edible button mushroom merely from the gill colour.

sections.title: Stem, ring and yellowing
sections.text: The relatively short, robust white stem may narrow or be slightly club-shaped toward its base rather than ending in a strong bulb. Its superior white ring is conspicuously complex, often with several folded layers. The stem base and cut flesh there rapidly stain vivid chrome yellow, and rubbing the cap can yellow it while fresh. An unpleasant phenolic, carbolic or iodine-like odour is often reported; its intensity varies among accounts.

sections.title: Habitat and record
sections.text: A saprobic species recorded chiefly in human-disturbed sites such as gardens, parks, flower beds and graveyards, sometimes under trees. A documented Sicilian collection was repeatedly observed in a small neglected garden flower bed, with a preserved Palermo herbarium voucher. European records are relatively scattered; fruiting is mostly autumnal, with some spring reports.

sections.title: Similar Agaricus
sections.text: A. xanthodermus and A. moelleri share yellowing and phenolic odours and belong to the same toxic yellow-staining group. A. pilatianus differs in its notably thickset habit, non-bulbous or tapered stem base and strongly folded ring, but these are comparative tendencies rather than a simple field test. Edible A. bisporus also has free gills that darken to chocolate, so that character alone cannot establish edibility. Taxonomic work places the yellow-staining Xanthodermatei among taxa of mild to substantial toxicity.

sections.title: About the plate
sections.text: The white-background plate illustrates a whole, squat, grey-brown scaly specimen with a multi-folded ring, a longitudinal section showing chrome-yellow staining concentrated at the stem base, a cap from above, and free pink-to-chocolate gills from below. The illustration represents typical reported characters; actual specimens vary.
